front: {{c1::Automatic}} processing is fast, parallel, and resistant to load after practice; {{c2::controlled}} processing is slow, serial, and capacity-limited.
why: Automatic vs controlled processing: foundational attention distinction, every year

front: {{c1::Broca's}} aphasia: nonfluent, agrammatic speech, intact comprehension; {{c2::Wernicke's}}: fluent but meaningless speech, poor comprehension.
why: Restates the Broca/Wernicke contrast card with extra descriptors

front: {{c1::Deductive}} reasoning moves from general premises to a certain conclusion; {{c2::inductive}} reasoning generalizes from cases to a probable rule.
why: Deductive vs inductive reasoning: secondary problem-solving distinction

front: {{c1::Divergent}} thinking generates many possible solutions and underlies creativity; {{c2::convergent}} thinking narrows toward the single best answer.
why: Divergent/convergent thinking: second-tier creativity distinction

front: {{c1::Inattentional blindness}} is missing an unexpected object while attending elsewhere; {{c2::change blindness}} is missing an alteration between two views.
why: Inattentional vs change blindness: commonly tested attention pair

front: {{c1::Prototype}} models compare an item with an averaged category ideal; {{c2::exemplar}} models compare it with stored individual instances.
why: Prototype vs exemplar categorization models are not on the AAMC outline

front: A 5-year-old says a tall thin glass holds more after water is poured from a short wide one. Which two preoperational limits does this show?
why: Conservation failure and centration: classic preoperational item every year

front: A child who once said 'went' now says 'goed' — {{c1::overregularization}}, evidence children extract grammatical {{c2::rules}}, not just imitations.
why: Overregularization as rule-learning evidence: commonly tested language milestone

front: A child with normal grammar and vocabulary cannot take turns, read sarcasm, or adjust tone to a listener. Which language component is impaired?
why: Pragmatics: language component secondary to phoneme/morpheme/syntax

front: A mental set is:
why: Mental set: AAMC-listed barrier to problem solving

front: A patient speaks fluently and comprehends well but cannot repeat phrases. Name the aphasia and the damaged tract.
why: Conduction aphasia/arcuate fasciculus completes the aphasia triad

front: A patient with dorsolateral prefrontal damage keeps sorting by color after the rule silently switches to shape. Name the error and the function lost.
why: WCST perseveration illustrates executive function; task detail secondary

front: A scale reads five pounds heavy every single time. It is {{c1::reliable}} but not {{c2::valid}}, showing reliability is necessary but not sufficient.
why: Reliable-but-not-valid scale: tested every year even though it is research methods

front: A stroke patient's speech is slurred but grammatically intact, and her writing is normal. Is this aphasia, dysarthria, or apraxia of speech?
why: Dysarthria vs apraxia of speech is clinical neurology beyond the MCAT

front: A toddler calls a zebra 'horse' — {{c1::assimilation}} into an existing schema; revising the schema to add zebras is {{c2::accommodation}}.
why: Assimilation vs accommodation: foundational Piaget, every year

front: After an election, people claim they 'knew it all along'. Name the bias and its danger for evaluating decisions.
why: Hindsight bias: commonly tested bias

front: After five reds at roulette, one bettor expects black is 'due'; another bets red for the 'streak'. Name each error.
why: Gambler's fallacy: plausible passage bias, not AAMC-listed

front: After heavy news coverage of a plane crash, people overestimate flying risk. Which heuristic, and what actually drives the estimate?
why: Availability heuristic in scenario form: the way AAMC asks it, every year

front: An 8-month-old searches at location A after watching a toy hidden at B. Name the error and its Piagetian stage.
why: A-not-B error: supporting detail on object permanence

front: Belief perseverance is:
why: Belief perseverance: explicitly named on the AAMC outline

front: Broca's area damage produces:
why: Subset restatement of the Broca/Wernicke contrast card

front: Cattell: {{c1::fluid}} intelligence (novel reasoning) declines with age, while {{c2::crystallized}} intelligence (accumulated knowledge) holds steady or grows.
why: Cattell attribution; the plain fluid/crystallized card carries the core

front: Chomsky's poverty of the stimulus argument: what does it claim, and what mechanism did he propose?
why: Chomsky poverty of stimulus and LAD: core nativist theory

front: Continuing a failing project because 'we've already invested so much' — name the fallacy and the normative rule it violates.
why: Sunk cost fallacy: secondary decision-making bias

front: Contrast algorithms and heuristics in problem solving, and name the heuristic of reducing distance to the goal stepwise.
why: Adds means-end analysis to the heuristic/algorithm distinction

front: Contrast Broca's and Wernicke's aphasia.
why: Broca vs Wernicke aphasia: tested on essentially every administration

front: Contrast fluid and crystallized intelligence.
why: Fluid vs crystallized intelligence: tested every year

front: Crystallized intelligence tends to:
why: One-sided restatement of the fluid/crystallized contrast card

front: Deaf adults who first acquired sign language after puberty show persistent grammatical errors despite decades of fluent use. What does this support?
why: Late-signer study restates the sensitive-period point the Genie card makes

front: Define the availability and representativeness heuristics.
why: Availability and representativeness definitions: the two core AAMC heuristics

front: Distinguish confirmation bias from belief perseverance.
why: Confirmation bias vs belief perseverance: useful distinction of two covered biases

front: Duncker's candle problem demonstrates {{c1::functional fixedness}}; Luchins's water-jar problems demonstrate {{c2::mental set}} (Einstellung).
why: Named-task restatement of the mental set and functional fixedness cards

front: Even after spinning an obviously random wheel, people's estimates of unrelated quantities track the wheel's number. Name and explain the bias.
why: Anchoring and adjustment: commonly tested heuristic

front: Gardner's theory proposes:
why: Gardner is covered by the match-to-theorist intelligence card

front: How do Vygotsky's zone of proximal development and scaffolding challenge Piaget's picture of development?
why: Vygotsky ZPD/scaffolding vs Piaget: foundational cognitive-development contrast

front: How does hearing your own name in an unattended conversation challenge Broadbent's filter model, and what did Treisman propose instead?
why: Cocktail party effect and Broadbent/Treisman models: outline selective-attention content

front: In dichotic listening with shadowing, what do subjects retain from the unattended ear?
why: Dichotic listening finding: secondary selective-attention detail

front: In Simons and Chabris's study, half the viewers counting basketball passes missed a person in a gorilla suit. Name the phenomenon and its cousin.
why: Named-study restatement of the inattentional/change blindness card

front: In the Linda problem, why is 'feminist bank teller' judged likelier than 'bank teller', and what fallacy is this?
why: Conjunction fallacy: secondary representativeness example

front: IQ heritability is about 0.5-0.8 in adults. Why can't this explain average differences between groups?
why: Heritability within vs between groups: plausible reasoning step

front: Judging category membership by resemblance while ignoring category frequency — {{c1::base rate neglect}}, via the {{c2::representativeness}} heuristic.
why: Base rate neglect via representativeness: every-year heuristic item

front: List Piaget's four stages of cognitive development, in order.
why: Piaget four stages: foundational, tested every year

front: Match to theorist: a general factor g; eight relatively independent intelligences; analytical, creative, and practical intelligence.
why: Spearman/Gardner/Sternberg intelligence theories: on the outline

front: Match to theorist: language is shaped by reinforcement; language rests on an innate acquisition device; language emerges from scaffolded social interaction.
why: Skinner/Chomsky/interactionist language theories: tested every year

front: Modern IQ scores are set to a mean of {{c1::100}} and a standard deviation of {{c2::15}}, so roughly 68 percent of people fall between 85 and 115.
why: IQ mean 100/SD 15: normal-distribution reasoning appears often

front: Name and briefly define the three intelligences in Sternberg's triarchic theory.
why: Triarchic components: supporting detail on Sternberg

front: Physicians who report 90 percent certainty in a diagnosis are correct far less often. Name the bias and one strategy that actually reduces it.
why: Overconfidence: explicitly named on the AAMC outline

front: Piaget's {{c1::formal operational}} stage (about 12+) brings abstract, hypothetical-deductive reasoning, classically tested with the {{c2::pendulum}} task.
why: Formal operational abstract reasoning: commonly tested stage marker

front: Piaget's {{c1::sensorimotor}} stage (0-2 yrs) culminates in {{c2::object permanence}} and the onset of mental representation.
why: Sensorimotor object permanence: commonly tested stage marker

front: Prospect theory: losses loom larger than equivalent gains ({{c1::loss aversion}}), so choices reverse under different {{c2::framing}} of the same outcomes.
why: Loss aversion and framing (prospect theory): every-year decision content

front: Reading the word 'nurse' speeds recognition of 'doctor' but not of 'butter'. Name the effect and the memory model it supports.
why: Semantic priming/spreading activation: belongs to memory

front: Stern's ratio IQ = ({{c1::mental age}} / chronological age) x 100; modern tests instead use {{c2::deviation}} IQ normed to mean 100, SD 15.
why: Historical ratio-IQ formula; modern deviation IQ card covers what is tested

front: Subjects accept a logically invalid syllogism because its conclusion happens to be true in the real world. Name the effect and the failure it reveals.
why: Belief bias in syllogisms is not on the AAMC outline

front: The {{c1::availability}} heuristic judges frequency by ease of recall; the {{c2::representativeness}} heuristic judges probability by resemblance.
why: Restatement of the availability/representativeness definition card

front: The {{c1::Whorf (linguistic relativity)}} hypothesis says language shapes thought; evidence supports only the {{c2::weak}} version.
why: Whorf linguistic relativity, weak version: asked nearly every year

front: The Flynn effect describes:
why: Flynn effect: secondary intelligence fact

front: The same policy described as '200 saved' versus '400 will die' flips people from risk-averse to risk-seeking. Name the effect and the theory behind it.
why: Restatement of the loss aversion/framing prospect theory card

front: The smallest unit of sound is a {{c1::phoneme}}; the smallest unit of meaning is a {{c2::morpheme}}.
why: Phoneme vs morpheme: foundational language-component distinction

front: The Stroop task: why is naming the ink color of the word RED printed in blue so slow?
why: Stroop interference: standard automatic-vs-controlled example

front: The three mountains task reveals {{c1::egocentrism}} in Piaget's {{c2::preoperational}} stage (about 2-7 years).
why: Egocentrism/three mountains: classic preoperational marker

front: Trace the language timeline: cooing, babbling, first words, telegraphic speech — and what happens to babbling around 9-10 months?
why: Language milestone timeline: commonly tested

front: What can a concrete operational child (7-11) do that a preoperational child cannot, and what remains beyond them?
why: Concrete operational detail; the four-stages card carries the core

front: What did Herbert Simon mean by bounded rationality and satisficing?
why: Bounded rationality/satisficing is not on the AAMC outline

front: What does the case of Genie suggest about language acquisition, and what is the key interpretive caveat?
why: Genie critical-period case: standard language-acquisition evidence

front: What evidence led Spearman to propose general intelligence (g)?
why: Spearman g evidence: supporting detail on the theorist card

front: What is a heuristic and how does it differ from an algorithm?
why: Heuristic vs algorithm: foundational problem-solving distinction

front: What is confirmation bias?
why: Confirmation bias: tested every year

front: What is dual-process theory?
why: Dual-process System 1/2: foundational decision-making content

front: What is functional fixedness?
why: Functional fixedness: AAMC-listed barrier to problem solving

front: Which of the following best describes syntax?
why: Syntax definition: supporting detail on language components
